Jordan’s Retail Industry Faces Severe Financial Crisis Amid Sudden Credit Freeze

Amman – Jordan’s retail industry is grappling with a mounting financial crisis after a sudden credit freeze last week left dozens of firms unable to access crucial short-term funding. The event has sent shockwaves through the sector, forcing major chains and small independent retailers alike to scale back operations, delay payments to workers, and shutter some locations.

According to the Jordan Retail Association, the crisis began when several local lenders tightened lending criteria and halted new credit lines to retail businesses. “We have not seen anything like this in at least a decade,” said Association President Omar Al-Nawas. “With credit inaccessible, stores cannot restock shelves or manage cash flows. Many have had to suspend planned renovations or expansion projects.”

Retailers in Amman’s bustling downtown and major shopping centers in Irbid and Aqaba report sharp drops in inventory and rising uncertainty among employees. At the busy Al-Salam Mall, workers at Al-Riyad Stores said they were told their wages could be delayed. “We fear for our jobs,” said store clerk Mahmoud Abu Saleh, who has worked in the sector for six years. “The manager told us to expect shorter hours and less overtime until things improve.”

Industry analysts say the credit freeze hit as retailers were already struggling with sluggish consumer demand and rising costs. “This is a perfect storm,” said retail consultant Rania Saad. “Many companies borrowed to cover operating expenses, counting on steady turnover. Now, with credit lines frozen, they are squeezed from both sides.”

Several mid-sized chains, including Al-Karamah Mart and Jordan Value Stores, have reportedly closed some of their smaller branches, putting hundreds of jobs at risk. The Jordan Retail Workers Union said it has received over 350 complaints this week alone from staff worried about layoffs or wage delays. “Our members are anxious,” said Union Secretary-General Firas Haddad. “We urge companies to respect workers’ rights and the government to intervene to protect jobs.”

The Ministry of Industry and Trade said officials are in talks with retail leaders to assess the situation and explore support measures. “Our priority is to stabilize the sector and safeguard employment,” a spokesperson said.

As the crisis persists, many retailers are urging policymakers to facilitate emergency credit and provide temporary relief to help the industry weather the storm. “Without swift action, we risk seeing a wave of closures,” warned Al-Nawas. “The retail sector is at a critical crossroads.”
